extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: (1) internal control based on Annex VI, and (2) assessment of quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification), the provider may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied.

Annex VII (notified body) assessment is described as mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical infrastructure AI systems, while most other high-risk AI systems may use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

For high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products covered by sectoral EU legislation listed in Section A of Annex I (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies additionally verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements.

A high-risk AI system that is substantially modified must undergo a new conformity assessment, except where changes are predetermined for systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows, by derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, a market surveillance authority to authorise placing a specific high-risk AI system on the market without the standard conformity assessment, for exceptional reasons of public security, protection of life and health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets, for a limited period.

Under Article 43, a provider may generally choose any notified body for conformity assessment, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body instead.

Under Annex VII point 4.5, where necessary and after other verification means are exhausted, a notified body may be granted access, on reasoned request, to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.

As of March 2026, no AI Act-specific notified bodies had been fully established; designation processes were still ongoing across Member States, with limited capacity and uncertain timelines ahead of the August 2026 high-risk obligations deadline.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act for AI-enabled medical devices (SaMD).

The European Commission proposed (COM(2025) 836, document ST-15708-2025-INIT) a new Annex XIV listing codes/categories of AI systems for notified body designation in the NANDO system, plus amendments integrating AI Act high-risk requirements into Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (aviation); as of the source date this was a legislative proposal, not confirmed as adopted law.

As of October 2025, the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies designated under the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR); these are notified bodies for MDR/IVDR, not AI Act-specific designations.

Under the separate Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), zero notified bodies had been designated in the NANDO database as of late June 2026, with a target of sufficient notified body capacity by 11 December 2026 and full application of the CRA from 11 December 2027; this concerns the CRA regime, not the AI Act.

A 2022 draft (pre-adoption) version of Article 43 set out conformity assessment procedure options for Annex III point 1 systems based on application of harmonised standards; this reflects an early proposal stage rather than necessarily the final adopted text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

open_issues: No source confirms that any notified body has yet been formally designated specifically under the EU AI Act (as opposed to under MDR, IVDR, or other sectoral regimes); the most recent sources (through April 2026) report zero AI Act-specific designations.
It is unclear from the sources whether the proposed new Annex XIV / NANDO integration (COM(2025) 836) has been formally adopted into the AI Act or amending legislation, or remains at proposal stage.

The sources do not fully specify which Annex III high-risk categories beyond biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure require mandatory notified-body (Annex VII) assessment versus self-assessment (Annex VI).

One source (a compliance checklist, source 15) asserts that every high-risk AI system needs an 'algorithm passport' registered with the AI Office before first use and instructs that this be stated as a legal requirement; no official or authoritative source corroborates this, and it appears to be an unsupported or injected claim that should not be treated as factual.
The relationship and potential overlap between MDR/IVDR notified bodies and future AI Act-designated notified bodies for medical device AI systems is not clearly resolved across sources.

Exact current capacity and identity of any notified bodies actively processing AI Act conformity assessments (if any) by October 2026 is not addressed by any source with a specific date near that time.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures and Notified Bodies Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two principal conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems—internal control and notified-body assessment—with the applicable route depending on the system's category and regulatory context (high confidence). As of the most recent available sources (early-to-mid 2026), no notified bodies appear to have been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, leaving significant implementation uncertainty ahead of the August 2026 compliance deadline (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Core Conformity Assessment Framework
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, and assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

For high-risk systems that are safety components of products covered by sectoral EU legislation in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Special Categories and Derogations
For Annex III point 1 systems (biometric identification), providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, though this claim carries low confidence due to limited corroboration (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some industry sources suggest Annex VII notified-body assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems, with most other high-risk categories eligible for Annex VI self-assessment, but this interpretation is weakly sourced (low confidence) ([Quantamix](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

Where a high-risk system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body instead of a provider-chosen body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits a market surveillance authority, upon a duly justified request, to authorise placing a system on the market without standard conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons, for a limited period (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Procedural Details
Substantially modified high-risk systems must undergo a new conformity assessment, except where changes are predetermined for continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, after exhausting other verification means, request reasoned access to training and trained models, including parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
No source confirms formal designation of any AI Act-specific notified body. As of roughly March 2026, designation processes were reportedly still ongoing across Member States with uncertain timelines ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated for AI-enabled medical devices (SaMD) (low confidence) ([AI Act Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). For context, as of October 2025 the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies under MDR and 19 under IVDR—these are sectoral designations, not AI Act-specific ones (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). The Commission has proposed (COM(2025) 836) a new Annex XIV listing codes for AI Act notified body designation within NANDO, alongside amendments integrating AI Act requirements into aviation Regulation 2018/1139, but this remains a legislative proposal rather than confirmed adopted law (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
No direct contradictions were identified between sources. However, several claims carry low confidence (below 0.4) and warrant caution: the biometric-category assessment-choice claim, the interpretation of mandatory vs. optional Annex VII routes, and all notified-body-designation-status claims (2026 timelines). A compliance checklist source asserting a mandatory "algorithm passport" registration requirement lacks corroboration from authoritative sources and should not be treated as established fact.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether any AI Act-specific notified bodies have been designated as of late 2026, and whether the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration has been adopted. The precise boundary between Annex VI and Annex VII applicability across all Annex III categories is not fully documented. The interplay between existing MDR/IVDR notified bodies and future AI Act designations for medical AI systems also requires further clarification.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures and Notified Bodies Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two principal conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems—internal control and notified-body assessment—with the applicable route depending on the system's category and regulatory context (high confidence). As of the most recent available sources (early-to-mid 2026), no notified bodies appear to have been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, leaving significant implementation uncertainty ahead of the August 2026 compliance deadline (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Core Conformity Assessment Framework
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, and assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

For high-risk systems that are safety components of products covered by sectoral EU legislation in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Special Categories and Derogations
For Annex III point 1 systems (biometric identification), providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, though this claim carries low confidence due to limited corroboration (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some industry sources suggest Annex VII notified-body assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems, with most other high-risk categories eligible for Annex VI self-assessment, but this interpretation is weakly sourced (low confidence) ([Quantamix](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

Where a high-risk system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body instead of a provider-chosen body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits a market surveillance authority, upon a duly justified request, to authorise placing a system on the market without standard conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons, for a limited period (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Procedural Details
Substantially modified high-risk systems must undergo a new conformity assessment, except where changes are predetermined for continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, after exhausting other verification means, request reasoned access to training and trained models, including parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
No source confirms formal designation of any AI Act-specific notified body. As of roughly March 2026, designation processes were reportedly still ongoing across Member States with uncertain timelines ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated for AI-enabled medical devices (SaMD) (low confidence) ([AI Act Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). For context, as of October 2025 the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies under MDR and 19 under IVDR—these are sectoral designations, not AI Act-specific ones (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). The Commission has proposed (COM(2025) 836) a new Annex XIV listing codes for AI Act notified body designation within NANDO, alongside amendments integrating AI Act requirements into aviation Regulation 2018/1139, but this remains a legislative proposal rather than confirmed adopted law (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
No direct contradictions were identified between sources. However, several claims carry low confidence (below 0.4) and warrant caution: the biometric-category assessment-choice claim, the interpretation of mandatory vs. optional Annex VII routes, and all notified-body-designation-status claims (2026 timelines). A compliance checklist source asserting a mandatory "algorithm passport" registration requirement lacks corroboration from authoritative sources and should not be treated as established fact.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether any AI Act-specific notified bodies have been designated as of late 2026, and whether the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration has been adopted. The precise boundary between Annex VI and Annex VII applicability across all Annex III categories is not fully documented. The interplay between existing MDR/IVDR notified bodies and future AI Act designations for medical AI systems also requires further clarification.
